newsitem.title: POLAND: FEATURE - Polish textile firms look to new markets.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Polish textile firms look to new markets.

text.p: Polish textile firms, squeezed on Western export markets, are preparing to fight over promising domestic prospects and seek new openings in the former Soviet Union as they battle for survival.

Although much of the industry emerged in fair shape from its plunge into market realities after communism fell in 1989, manufacturers say old equipment and declining competitiveness mean testing times ahead, not only for small firms.

"There really was a break-down in favourable market conditions at the turn of the year," said Wlodzimierz Szydlo, chief executive of Bytom SA, although he added that domestic sales had shown strong growth in recent months.
Ominous signs appeared late last year after cold and rain put consumers off buying new clothes in the summer and autumn seasons -- swelling inventories and tying up capital.
Polish manufacturers also reported a rise in cheap and often illegal imports of ready goods from the Far East.
Meanwhile the growing obsolescence of plant and equipment and rises in electricity prices, compounded by a strong zloty currency hampering exports, have undermined competitiveness.
COMPETITION CUTS PROFITS

Rivalry from the Ukraine and the former Yugolavia, which have cheaper labour, has cut into the profits of a previously thriving business of sub-contracting to make finished goods for major Western brand-name manufacturers.
But the picture is far from gloomy across the sector.

"A positive trend which emerged recently is the increasing number of firms with positive financial results, though profits are smaller than in past years," said Zbigniew Wawraszek, Director of the Polish Textile Industry Chamber (PIPT).
"This shows companies have been able to adapt to changing market conditions," he told Reuters in Poland's historic textiles capital and second largest city, Lodz.
Chamber figures show that, in the first nine months of last year, 65 percent of textile companies showed a net profit, and average profitability on sales was 3.9 percent.
Wawraszek said the picture varied according to the branch, with clothing and knitted goods doing fine, and linen badly. The chamber estimates 30 percent of firms could be in trouble.
FIRMS FORESEE SECTOR SHAKEOUT
Some of Poland's big names are upbeat.
"I am a moderate optimist about the situation in the textile industry," said Ryszard Polanski, chief executive of Wolczanka SA.
But finance director Roman Matlok of Pabia Moden, who said his firm was doing good business making coats and suits under licence to Pierre Cardin, said a sector shakeout was under way.
"There are too many clothing firms with excess capacity and some will definitely go under," he said, adding that these included big firms with high fixed costs and low flexibility.
The Chamber says the industry needs a $2.0-$2.5 billion revamp to be competitive after Poland joins the European Union.
"We estimate about 30 percent of machinery is completely obsolete and has to be completely replaced," said Jerzy Wojtkowski, head of the PIPT chamber's management board.
"The cost of technical restructuring of the whole sector is estimated at $2.0-2.5 billion and our projection is that 30 percent of this should come from firms themselves," he said.
The rest should come from long-term credits, especially provided by EU countries which will supply 90 percent of the new equipment, notably Germany, Italy and France.
GOVERNMENT HELP SOUGHT
Wojtkowski said Poland's government had to help by obtaining favourable credit lines and providing guarantees.
"At present firms are managing quite well. About 20 percent are in good financial condition and 50 percent are satisfactory," Wojtkowski said.
But he said companies were having to face major unfair competition from the Far East, much of which was smuggled, brought in at dumping prices or with avoidance of tax.

"The scale of this is huge. For instance cotton imports are twice domestic production, with silk it is four times greater," he said, alleging that 90 percent of imported goods were underpriced and 25 percent were unregistered.
He said the government had a major role to play here and in easing the tax demands on Polish firms.
The chamber says that, if its programme is implemented, by the year 2000 production will double and energy use will fall by half with profits from exports rising accordingly.
But Polish firms accept their future is in their own hands, especially their ability to switch to the domestic market.

"Those firms that now make just completed goods for export (to the West) will disappear in a few years, while those that find the right proportion of such contracted exports and domestic sales will survive," said Pabia Moden's Matlok.
FIRMS LOOK TO HOME MARKET
Manufacturers said they would not press for the zloty exchange rate to be reduced to stimulate exports.
Instead they are girding up for a fight at home, creating or boosting distribution networks, improving design and market research and trying to slash costs further.

"There are as yet unpenetrated sectors within the country which have great potential demand for domestic products," said Vistula's Tabaka, whose company is setting up a network of dedicated outlets along with Wolczanka and hopes Prochnik SA will join the scheme.

Chiefs of large firms said it was important to identify niches on the domestic market, build up brand recognition with better marketing and compete for the expensive, quality end of the market while trying to cut costs.
"We know we have to squeeze costs at Wolczanka. For several months we have therefore been restructuring, which has involved lay-offs of staff," said Polanski.
"It's better to make 50 people redundant now than 500 in half a year's time," said Polanski whose firm is the biggest clothing producer in Poland with 3,500 employees.
EXPORT DRIVE TO EAST
Apart from the internal market, firms are also looking to to the East, which according to the chamber's figures, now accounts for only 3.7 percent of Poland's textile exports.
"In Vistula, we are banking on moving part of our export from West to East," said Tabaka, adding that Vistula and Wolczanka were opening a new shop in Russia's Kaliningrad enclave.
Wolczanka's Polanski said that if tests of the Russian market proved successful the company would open wholesale outlets there and try to penetrate deeper to Moscow itself.
"If sales of our shirts grow there, it will be cheaper to make them on the spot than transport them from Poland," Polanski added.
